final_answer:
Short answer: On the stated facts, probably yes as to the dispersal order and the failure-to-disperse arrests, though the answer is fact-dependent and the remedy (damages vs. injunction vs. criminal defense) is subject to significant hurdles. A dispersal order issued only because of generalized worries about traffic and 'potential escalation,' with no identified imminent violence or property damage, is hard to justify under the First Amendment, and an arrest for disobeying such an order lacks a lawful predicate.

1. Framework. Sidewalk/plaza protest on public property is core protected expression in a traditional public forum. Government may impose content-neutral time, place and manner restrictions that are narrowly tailored to significant interests (Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972), which also recognizes that peaceful demonstration may be curtailed when it actually or imminently disrupts, and that vague standards invite arbitrary enforcement). Peaceful assemblies cannot be dispersed or criminalized merely because of anticipated hostile reaction or the unpopularity of the message: Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963); Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965) (I confirmed these only through search summaries, not full texts).

2. Illinois/Chicago law. The state failure-to-disperse offense is tied to mob action: a participant in a mob action who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer commits a Class A misdemeanor (720 ILCS 5/25-1). Mob action requires force/violence disturbing the peace, or assembly intended to commit a crime or do violence. Chicago Mun. Code 8-4-010 criminalizes failure to obey a lawful dispersal order issued by an identifiable peace officer 'under circumstances where three or more persons are committing acts of disorderly conduct in the immediate vicinity, which acts are likely to cause substantial harm.' Thus the predicate is acts of disorderly conduct likely to cause substantial harm, not mere traffic inconvenience or verbal arguments. Occasional stepping into the street and a couple of verbal arguments, without more, likely do not meet that predicate, though stepping into the roadway could support separate narrow charges (e.g., pedestrian/traffic or permit offenses) and, if it was substantial and obstructive, could bolster a lawful order. I did not verify the full current text of these provisions on the official sites beyond search excerpts.

3. Seventh Circuit. Schirmer v. Nagode, 621 F.3d 581 (7th Cir. 2010), addressed the Chicago dispersal provision: the court read it as permitting dispersal when conduct of three or more people threatens imminent physical injury or property destruction, noted that authorizing dispersal for mere 'serious inconvenience' would invite arbitrary application, and treated the arrests there as apparently specious but an isolated misuse, which defeated pre-enforcement standing. This supports the view that a dispersal order not grounded in imminent harm is unlawful as applied, but the case itself did not grant relief. (Summary from search results; full opinion not retrieved because the fetch was blocked.)

4. Application. Facts: peaceful, signs, chanting, mostly on sidewalk, a few verbal arguments, order after a couple of hours, justified by traffic and potential escalation. No identified violence, threats, or imminent property damage. Under Edwards/Cox and Schirmer's reading of the ordinance, generalized concern about escalation is not enough, and the order lacked a lawful predicate; arrests for noncompliance would then lack probable cause under the ordinance and violate the First Amendment as applied. Counterpoints: police may regulate actual street blockage, and a court may credit evidence of real traffic obstruction or escalation, a fact question; officers might claim arguable probable cause for some other offense (Devenpeck v. Alford rule that the arrest's validity need not rest on the stated offense; not researched here); and civil damages claims face qualified immunity and, for Monell liability against the City, require policy/custom. Individual arrestees have the usual defenses in prosecution (dismissal as an unlawful order/insufficient evidence).

5. Unresolved: whether the plaza was a permitted event or had other restrictions; actual extent of street blockage; whether the protest had violent elements; content of the order; any other applicable ordinances (permit, parade, traffic); post-2025 case law; and the unmerged state statutory text. Bottom line: the dispersal and arrests likely violated the First Amendment if the only grounds were those stated, but outcome depends on facts and on qualified immunity.

authorities.title: Mob Action
authorities.proposition: Failure to withdraw when commanded by peace officer is an offense only for a participant in a mob action (force/violence or intent to commit offense).

authorities.title: Disorderly conduct
authorities.proposition: Failure to obey a lawful dispersal order requires three or more persons committing disorderly acts in the vicinity likely to cause substantial harm.

authorities.title: Schirmer v. Nagode
authorities.proposition: Chicago dispersal provision read to require imminent physical/property harm; dispersal for mere inconvenience risks arbitrary application; isolated misuse defeated standing.

authorities.citation: Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972)
authorities.title: Grayned v. City of Rockford
authorities.proposition: Reasonable time/place/manner regulation allowed; vague standards invite arbitrary enforcement.

authorities.title: Edwards v. South Carolina
authorities.proposition: Peaceful protesters who refused to disperse could not be convicted of breach of peace.

authorities.title: Cox v. Louisiana
authorities.proposition: Breach-of-peace laws cannot be used against peaceable demonstrations on potential for violence.

claims.text: A dispersal order based only on generalized traffic and escalation concerns, absent imminent harm, likely violates the First Amendment and lacks a lawful predicate.
Failure-to-disperse arrests require a lawful order issued amid disorderly conduct likely to cause substantial harm (Chicago) or mob action (Illinois); the facts do not clearly show either.
Actual street obstruction can be regulated, and damages remedies face qualified immunity/Monell hurdles, so outcome is fact-dependent.
